stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 10 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 303 K and 1 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 40.0 mL of 0.15 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.4 \times 10^{-4}) with 0.14 M NaOH.
8.2 g of $$\ce{NaOH}$$ dissolves in 66 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 9.1 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Ni electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$ and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Cu^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Ni^{2+} + 2e- -> Ni}$$ E° = -0.25 V; $$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e- -> Cu}$$ E° = 0.34 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Si (Z = 14) and P (Z = 15) are compared.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 39.2 g. The actual yield is 27.8 g. What is the percent yield?
What is the pH of a 0.01 M solution of $$\ce{KOH}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 1 × 0.01 M; pH = 14 − pOH.

questions.stem: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Zn²⁺] is increased. What happens to the cell potential?

options.why: Correct. A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.explanation: A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 3.3. A mixture has [A] = 0.7 M, [B] = 0.6 M and [C] = 0.4 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.381
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.381, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.381
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.952

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{MgF2}$$ or $$\ce{NaF}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{NaF}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{NaF}$$, because its ions have larger charges

questions.explanation: MgF2 has ion charges 2 and 1; NaF has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 6.7. In a solution at pH 5.1, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: How many formula units or molecules are in 131 g of $$\ce{NaCl}$$?

options.why: Correct. Convert grams to moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 59 kJ/mol, the transition state at 127 kJ/mol and the products at 92 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 68, ΔH = 33, reverse Ea = 35 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: A solid melts at 1,710 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely:

options.text: An ionic solid that conducts as a solid
options.why: Ionic solids do not conduct as solids.
Molecular solids melt at low temperatures.

questions.stem: A 17.8 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 27.6 mL of 0.143 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).
He has a larger molar mass (4 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: He 4, N2 28, O2 32, H2 2.02.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.124 mol of solute in enough water to make 774 mL of solution?
A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0119 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
A reaction has K = 50. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 1.66 mol of gas in a 39 L container at 427 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 3.5. In a solution at pH 4.4, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -287 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -189 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.92 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 354 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
What is the oxidation number of N in $$\ce{NH3}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.231 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
Which is the ground-state electron configuration of aluminum (Al, Z = 13)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 13 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).
He has a larger molar mass (4 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: CO2 44, He 4, H2 2.02, O2 32.

questions.stem: 14 mL of 8.7 M solution is diluted to 302 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.41 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 335 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
What is the mass percent of Fe in $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$?

options.why: That is the percent of the other elements.
There are 2 atoms of Fe in the formula.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest acid?

options.why: Correct. More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.explanation: More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.05 M solution of formic acid (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 229 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: Why does increasing temperature increase reaction rate?

options.text: A larger fraction of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{SO2}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.why: Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel
Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.

options.text: Nonpolar, because it has no polar bonds
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

questions.explanation: SO2 is bent; the dipoles do not cancel.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: In HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.065 mol of solute in enough water to make 728 mL of solution?
How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{PCl3}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: 187 g of water at 87 °C is mixed with 93 g of water at 17 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.9 mol N₂, 0.6 mol O₂ and 0.7 mol Ar at a total pressure of 2.2 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 6.35) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 25.6 mL. What is the pH after 12.8 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of lithium shows two peaks: mass 6 with relative abundance 47% and mass 7 with 53%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.74) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 57.6 mL. What is the pH after 28.8 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 98 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 24 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 270 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 17. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: Why are metals good conductors of electricity?

options.text: Their ions move freely in the solid
options.why: Ions are fixed in the lattice.

options.text: Their valence electrons are delocalized and free to move

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: N2 28, H2 2.02, Ar 40, O2 32.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.68 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: Adding an inert gas to a reaction mixture at constant volume does what to the equilibrium?

options.text: Shifts it toward more gas moles
Nothing; partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged
Shifts it toward fewer gas moles

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: A 33.3 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 37.3 mL of 0.268 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: A compound (hydrogen peroxide) is 5.93% H, 94.1% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to HO; the molecular formula is H2O2.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 4 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}$$, which has 12 electrons.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$$, 48 g of $$\ce{CH4}$$ reacts with 88 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{CO2}$$ can form?

options.why: Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Not all of both reactants reacts.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 11 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -4.44; K = 0.0118. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.3 M and [I₂] = 1.1 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.7 M. What is K?
A buffer contains 0.22 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.2) and 0.27 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.07 mol of NaOH is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.
Correct. First react: OH⁻ converts HA to A⁻. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.
E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -6 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 2.42; K = 11.3. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{CaF2}$$ is 3.9 \times 10^{-11}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
When a reaction involving 0.067 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 167 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 8.2 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 5720 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 2.285 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in ln[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: X → Y + Z. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Exothermic: the solution warmed, so energy was released.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Ni²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.01 M F⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with F⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of P.
Explain why the 1s peak of P has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Si.

rubric.criterion: P has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: P has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Si: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
